paragraphs: Both creator and creation seek well-being, not suffering. Yet limited knowledge and foresight leave us vulnerable to accidents, harm we inflict on one another, and circumstances we do not fully understand. Hardship can make joy and meaning seem distant, but the abilities we inherit from the creator enable us to learn from painful experiences and help prevent similar hardship.

Removing avoidable suffering and learning from all suffering are wise uses of intelligence that honor the creator’s likeness within us. Meaning can lie in the suffering itself as well as in our response. A painful experience may reveal an unknown danger and become a warning that protects others. Understanding does not guarantee prevention, but it begins our effort to investigate causes, relieve harm, and prevent recurrence. Recognizing the good that may emerge from hardship can help us endure it.

Earlier thinkers offer distinct perspectives. Aeschylus portrays “learning through suffering” within a divine order [54]; Aristotle grounds practical wisdom in experience of particular circumstances [32]. Confucius emphasizes reflection and the correction of mistakes [36], while the Chinese tradition of jian takes history as a mirror for learning from past failures and suffering. Dewey shows how difficulty can prompt inquiry and the testing of solutions [55]. Frankl explores meaning amid unavoidable suffering while urging the removal of avoidable suffering [38].

Learning from suffering is a shared responsibility of all humanity. We fulfill this responsibility by expanding our shared knowledge and wisdom, passing what we learn to future generations, and applying it to prevent recurring harm. To neglect these lessons is to risk repeating preventable harm and squander the intelligence entrusted to us. Our common calling demands more than endurance: it calls us to turn painful experience into understanding and protection, promoting creation’s well-being and extending the creator’s nurturing presence into the world.
